title: War, Peace, Governance and the Earth: Verses in Context
bigQuestion: When the same verse is quoted to justify violence and to forbid it, what do context, occasion and the tradition's own rules add to the reading?

story.title: The Verse and the Sentence After It
story.kicker: A scholar and a terrorist quote the same nine words. Everything depends on what each one says next.
paragraphs: In the fall of 2014, a video circulated online. A masked man read a line from Surah 9, At-Tawbah, 'Repentance,' verse 5: slay the idolaters wherever you find them. He stopped there. The camera cut to a black flag. That week, in a lecture hall in the Chicago suburbs, a scholar trained at Al-Azhar in Cairo read the same verse aloud in Arabic to a room of students. Then he kept reading.

He read the rest of verse 5, which says that if they repent and establish prayer and pay the alms, leave their way free. He read verse 6, which says that if any of the idolaters seeks protection, grant it and escort him to a place of safety. He read verse 4, which says a treaty with those who have kept it must be honored to its term. Then he read verse 13, which describes the people in question as those who broke their oaths and attacked first.

'Now,' he said, 'you have read the passage. He read a sentence.' He explained that Muslim tradition places these verses in the year 631, after a group of Meccan tribes had broken a treaty. He said the classical commentators, from al-Tabari to Ibn Kathir, read it as an order about those particular tribes at that particular time, and that jurists of every school tied fighting to a legitimate authority, to just cause and to strict limits on whom a fighter could harm.

A student raised her hand. 'But the man in the video is a Muslim too. Why is your reading right and his wrong?' The scholar nodded. 'That is the correct question,' he said. 'I will not tell you what to believe. I will tell you what the tradition has said for fourteen centuries, and I will show you the rules it built. Then you can judge who is reading and who is cutting.' That fall, more than a hundred Muslim scholars signed an open letter making the same argument, point by point, to the group in the video.

This chapter reads the Qur'an's most quoted verses on fighting, on rulers and on the earth in their contexts: the occasions Muslim tradition gives them, the sentences around them, and the rules scholars derived from them. It ends with two modern documents in which Muslim leaders set out, in public, how they read their own book.
story.think: The scholar said the difference between his reading and the video's was 'reading and cutting.' What is lost when a verse is quoted without the verses around it? Does that apply to other texts you know?

lessons.title: Permission and Its Limits
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an's first verses on fighting frame it as a defense against those who attack, and 2:190 forbids beginning hostilities.
reading: Muslim tradition says that during the Mecca years, before 622, Muhammad's followers were told to bear persecution without fighting back. The first *permission* to fight, most commentators say, is 22:39–40, Al-Hajj: permission is given to those who are fought because they have been wronged, who were driven from their homes for saying their Lord is God. The verse adds that if God did not check one people by another, monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques would be destroyed. Commentators note that the verse names the houses of worship of several faiths.

The fullest early statement is 2:190–194, Al-Baqarah. Verse 190, in Pickthall's 1930 translation, reads: 'Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors.' Verse 191 tells the believers to fight the Meccans who had driven them out, but not at the sacred mosque unless attacked there first. Verse 192 says that if they cease, God is forgiving. Verse 193 sets the goal as ending persecution, and verse 194 restates a limit: respond in kind and no more.

Muslim tradition ties these verses to the year 628, when Muhammad and his followers set out to visit Mecca on pilgrimage and feared the Meccans would attack them in the sacred months. Classical commentators such as al-Tabari (d. 923) read 'begin not hostilities' as a ban on fighting those who do not fight, and many listed women, children, the old and monks as people not to be attacked. Some later jurists argued that verse 190's limit was abrogated by Surah 9; others, including many modern scholars, hold that it was never abrogated and governs all the rest.

This disagreement about abrogation is the hinge of the whole modern debate. Read one way, the Qur'an's rule is defense and restraint, with 9:5 a special case. Read the other way, 9:5 replaced the earlier limits. Both readings have classical support, and describing them fairly means showing that Muslims have argued about this since the first centuries.

words.d: the verse 22:39, which Muslim commentators read as the first allowance to fight, for those who were wronged and driven from their homes
one who begins hostilities; 2:190 says God does not love aggressors
four months of the Arabian calendar in which fighting was traditionally forbidden

look.title: Begin Not Hostilities
look.text: Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:190, Al-Baqarah, Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Who is to be fought, according to this verse, and who is not? How would a reader who thinks the verse was later abrogated read it differently from one who thinks it governs all the rest?

check.q: What does 2:190 say about who may be fought?
choices: Anyone who is not a Muslim
Only the tribes of Medina
Those who fight against the believers; it forbids beginning hostilities
No one; the verse forbids all fighting
check.why: The verse limits fighting to those who fight and says God does not love aggressors.

check.q: Which verse do most commentators read as the first permission to fight?
choices: 1:1, the opening of the Fatiha
112:1, on God's oneness
2:282, on debts
22:39, for those who were wronged and driven from their homes
check.why: 22:39–40 in Al-Hajj grants permission to those who are fought because they were wronged.

check.q: What is the main disagreement among scholars about 2:190?
choices: Whether its limits were abrogated by Surah 9 or govern all later verses
Whether it was revealed in Mecca or Baghdad
Whether it mentions prayer
Whether it belongs in the Qur'an at all
check.why: Some jurists held 2:190 was abrogated; many others, classical and modern, hold it was never abrogated.

lessons.title: The Sword Verse in Context
lessons.mainIdea: Qur'an 9:5, the so-called sword verse, addresses treaty-breaking Meccan tribes in 631, and its own surrounding verses set conditions and exceptions.
reading: Surah 9, At-Tawbah, is the only surah that does not open with the basmala, 'In the name of God.' Muslim tradition dates most of it to 630–631, the last years of Muhammad's life, after Mecca had submitted and the Muslim community had become the main power in Arabia. Its opening verses declare that God and the messenger are free of obligation toward idolaters who have broken their treaties, and give them four months' notice. Verse 4 excepts those who have kept their treaties: honor them to their term.

Then comes verse 5, which classical jurists nicknamed the *sword verse*. It says that when the sacred months have passed, the believers should fight the idolaters wherever they find them, seize them and besiege them; but if they repent, establish prayer and pay the alms, then let them go their way, for God is forgiving. Verse 6 adds that if any idolater asks for protection, he must be granted it, hear the Qur'an and be escorted to safety. Verse 13 describes the target group as people who broke their oaths and attacked first.

Commentators from al-Tabari to Ibn Kathir (d. 1373) read the verse as addressing the Arab tribes who had broken the treaty of Hudaybiyya, made in 628. Some medieval jurists argued that it abrogated every earlier verse urging patience or peace; counts of how many verses it supposedly cancelled ran into the dozens. Others, including the Andalusian Ibn Rushd (d. 1198) in his survey of the schools' disputes, reported both views without settling them. Most modern Muslim scholars reject the wide abrogation reading and hold that 9:5 concerns a specific enemy at a specific time.

A student who reads only verse 5 sees a command to fight. A student who reads verses 1 to 13 sees a declaration of war against treaty-breakers, with notice, exceptions for those who kept faith, a route to peace through repentance, and safe passage for anyone who asks. Which of those readings the tradition chose was never a single answer, and the choice still shapes arguments today.

words.d: the jurists' nickname for Qur'an 9:5, which commands fighting treaty-breaking idolaters after the sacred months
the phrase 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate,' which opens every surah except the ninth
the treaty of 628 between Muhammad and the Meccans, whose breaking Muslim tradition gives as the occasion of Surah 9

look.title: Grant Him Protection
look.text: Right after the sword verse, 9:6 says that if any of the idolaters seeks the believers' protection, they should protect him so that he may hear the word of God, and then convey him to a place where he is safe, because these are people who do not know.
look.cite: Qur'an 9:6, At-Tawbah, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: How does verse 6 change the meaning of verse 5 when the two are read together? Why might a speaker who wants to justify violence stop reading at verse 5?

check.q: According to Muslim tradition, whom does 9:5 address?
choices: All non-Muslims for all time, as every commentator agrees
Meccan tribes that had broken the treaty of Hudaybiyya, around 631
The Jewish tribes of Medina in 622
The Byzantine emperor
check.why: Classical commentators tie the verse to the treaty-breaking tribes of Arabia in the Prophet's last years.

check.q: What does 9:6 require the believers to do?
choices: Fight the idolaters at the sacred mosque
Collect the alms tax from all of Arabia
Protect any idolater who asks for protection and escort him to safety
Open the surah with the basmala
check.why: Verse 6, right after the sword verse, grants safe passage to anyone who seeks protection.

check.q: What did some medieval jurists claim about 9:5 that most modern Muslim scholars reject?
choices: That it was revealed in Mecca
That it concerns fasting
That it was written by al-Tabari
That it abrogated every earlier verse urging patience or peace
check.why: The wide abrogation reading had classical supporters, but Ibn Rushd reported both views, and most modern scholars read 9:5 as specific to its occasion.

lessons.title: The People of the Book and the Poll Tax
lessons.mainIdea: Qur'an 9:29 commands fighting certain People of the Book until they pay the jizya, and jurists built from it the status of protected non-Muslim communities.
reading: Verse 9:29 turns from the idolaters to some of the *People of the Book*, the Qur'an's term for Jews and Christians. It commands fighting those among them who do not believe in God and the last day and do not follow the religion of truth, until they pay the *jizya* and are subdued. Muslim tradition ties the verse to the year 630 and the expedition to Tabuk on the Byzantine border, when Muhammad expected a Byzantine attack. The verse does not name a people; commentators debated whether it meant the Byzantines and their Arab allies or a wider group.

From this verse, together with the Prophet's treaties with Christian and Jewish towns, jurists built the status of the *dhimmi*: a non-Muslim under Muslim rule who paid the jizya, a poll tax, and in return kept his religion, property and community courts and was exempt from military service. Historians describe the system as more tolerant than most of medieval Europe and, at the same time, as a system of legal inequality, with restrictions that varied widely by ruler and century. Both descriptions are accurate.

Classical jurists disagreed on details: whether the tax was a penalty or a fee for protection, whether Hindus and Zoroastrians counted as People of the Book, and how much the rate should be. Modern Muslim scholars mostly hold that the dhimmi system belonged to a world of religious empires and that equal citizenship in a modern state serves the Qur'an's aim of justice better. The 2016 Marrakesh Declaration, signed by hundreds of Muslim scholars, argued exactly that, citing the Prophet's charter with the people of Medina.

Reading 9:29 in a public school means noting three things: what the verse says, whom Muslim tradition says it addressed, and how the tradition turned it into an institution that changed over time and is now widely reconsidered. It also means noting that a few modern extremist groups have revived the tax as a tool of terror, and that mainstream Muslim scholars have publicly rejected that use.

words.d: the Qur'an's term for Jews and Christians, and by extension other communities with a scripture
a poll tax paid by non-Muslims under Muslim rule, mentioned in 9:29
a protected non-Muslim under classical Muslim rule, who paid the jizya and kept his religion and community law

look.title: Two Historians, One Institution
look.text: Historian A: 'For most of the Middle Ages, a Jew or Christian was safer under Muslim rule than a Jew or Muslim under Christian rule; the dhimmi system let communities keep their faith, courts and property.' Historian B: 'The dhimmi system was legal inequality: a tax for being non-Muslim, limits on building and dress, and no equal say in government.' Both are describing the same institution.
look.prompt: How can both statements be accurate? What questions would you ask about a particular time and place before deciding how the system worked there?

check.q: What occasion does Muslim tradition give for 9:29?
choices: The expedition to Tabuk in 630, when a Byzantine attack was expected
The battle of Badr in 624
The first revelation in the cave
The conquest of Spain
check.why: Commentators tie the verse to Tabuk on the Byzantine frontier in the Prophet's last years.

check.q: In classical law, what did a dhimmi receive in exchange for the jizya?
choices: Full equality with Muslims in every matter
Protection, the right to keep his religion and community courts, and exemption from military service
Nothing; the tax was a fine with no return
A seat in the caliph's council
check.why: The dhimmi status combined protection and community autonomy with legal inequality.

check.q: What did the Marrakesh Declaration of 2016 argue?
choices: That the jizya must be revived everywhere
That 9:29 is not part of the Qur'an
That equal citizenship for non-Muslims serves the Qur'an's aims better than the old dhimmi system
That only Byzantines were People of the Book
check.why: Hundreds of Muslim scholars signed the declaration, citing the Prophet's charter of Medina, in favor of equal citizenship.

lessons.title: Incline to Peace: Rules of War
lessons.mainIdea: Qur'an 8:61 tells the Prophet to accept peace when offered, and classical jurists built rules of war that limit who may fight, why and whom they may harm.
reading: Surah 8, Al-Anfal, 'The Spoils of War,' is tied by Muslim tradition to the battle of Badr in 624, the first battle between the Muslims of Medina and the Meccans. Amid verses about courage and the division of spoils sits 8:61, which tells the Prophet that if the enemy inclines toward *peace*, he should incline toward it too and trust in God. Verse 62 adds that if they mean to deceive, God is enough for him. Commentators read the pair as a command to take peace when it is offered even at the risk of being tricked.

From verses like these, from the Prophet's practice and from the instructions attributed to the first caliph Abu Bakr, jurists built the *rules of war*. Muslim tradition reports that Abu Bakr, sending an army to Syria around 632, told the soldiers not to kill women, children or the old, not to cut down fruit trees, not to destroy homes, and to leave monks in their cells alone. Historians note that the report's wording varies across sources and cannot be confirmed, but jurists cited it for centuries as law.

The classical rules held that only a legitimate authority could declare war, that the enemy must be offered terms first, that noncombatants could not be targeted, that captives must be fed and could not be killed for being captives, and that treaties bound the community even against its interest. A well-known chapter in Ibn Rushd's handbook compares the schools on each of these points. The rules were not always followed, as historians of any tradition's wars will note, but they were the law that jurists taught.

Modern Muslim scholars, and international lawyers who study the tradition, point out that these rules overlap heavily with the Geneva Conventions: distinction between soldiers and civilians, humane treatment of prisoners, no unnecessary destruction. That overlap is a main argument in the scholars' answers to extremist groups, which the last lesson of this chapter takes up.

words.d: in 8:61, what the Prophet is told to accept when the enemy inclines to it
the classical jurists' limits on who may declare war, on whom may be harmed, and on how captives and treaties are handled
a person who is not fighting, such as a child, a woman, an old person or a monk, whom the classical rules protect

look.title: If They Incline to Peace
look.text: Verse 8:61 tells the Prophet that if the enemy inclines toward peace, he should incline toward it too and put his trust in God, who hears and knows. The next verse says that if they intend to deceive him, God is sufficient for him.
look.cite: Qur'an 8:61–62, Al-Anfal, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: The verse asks for peace to be accepted even at the risk of deception. What does that suggest about how the tradition weighs peace against safety?

check.q: What does 8:61 command?
choices: To fight until all enemies are destroyed
To divide the spoils of Badr equally
To fast during the sacred months
To incline to peace when the enemy inclines to it
check.why: The verse in Al-Anfal tells the Prophet to accept peace when it is offered and trust in God.

check.q: Which of these did the classical rules of war forbid?
choices: Targeting noncombatants such as women, children and monks
Offering the enemy terms before fighting
Feeding captives
Keeping treaties
check.why: Jurists held that noncombatants may not be targeted; the other three were duties, not prohibitions.

check.q: How do historians treat the instructions attributed to Abu Bakr?
choices: As a document in Abu Bakr's own handwriting
As a report whose wording varies and cannot be confirmed, though jurists cited it as law
As a forgery from the twentieth century
As part of the Qur'an
check.why: The report is well attested in later sources but its exact words differ, so historians describe it cautiously.

lessons.title: The Meanings of Jihad
lessons.mainIdea: Jihad means striving, and the Qur'an and Muslim tradition use it for inner effort, for speaking truth and for fighting under rules, in senses that Muslims weigh differently.
reading: The Arabic word *jihad* means striving or struggle. In the Qur'an it is often paired with 'in the way of God.' In some verses it clearly means armed fighting; in others it means effort of a different kind. Verse 25:52, Al-Furqan, a Mecca surah from before any battle, tells the Prophet to strive against the unbelievers with 'it,' which commentators take to mean the Qur'an itself: a jihad of argument. Verse 29:69, also from Mecca, promises guidance to those who strive for God's sake. The Qur'an uses a different word, qital, when it means fighting specifically.

Muslim tradition adds more senses. A saying widely quoted in Sufi and popular literature has the Prophet, returning from battle, say that the community has come back from the lesser jihad to the greater one, the struggle against the self. Many hadith scholars, including Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328), judged that report weak or unfounded; Sufi readers and many modern Muslims cite it anyway as true to the Qur'an's spirit. Another hadith, better attested, calls speaking a just word before a tyrant the best jihad.

The jurists' jihad was the armed one, and they treated it as a collective duty under a legitimate ruler, bound by the rules of war. Sunni law manuals placed the chapter on jihad among the duties of the state, not of the individual. Shia jurists mostly held that offensive jihad required the Imam and was suspended during his absence. Neither tradition, in its classical form, allowed private individuals to declare war, which is one point on which scholars' answers to extremists rest.

In modern usage the word has been pulled in every direction: by militants who claim it, by governments that use it for national wars, by Muslim writers who stress the inner struggle, and by non-Muslims who translate it simply as 'holy war,' a phrase with no exact Arabic original. A careful reader notes which sense a speaker means and which texts he cites for it.

words.d: striving or struggle, in the Qur'an usually 'in the way of God'; it can mean inner effort, argument or armed fighting
the Qur'an's specific word for fighting, distinct from jihad
the struggle against the self, named in a widely quoted report that many hadith scholars judge weak

look.title: One Word, Three Verses
look.text: 25:52 (Mecca, before any battle): strive against them with it, a mighty striving; commentators say 'it' is the Qur'an. 29:69 (Mecca): those who strive for Us, We guide to Our paths. 9:41 (Medina, tied to the Tabuk campaign): go forth, light or heavy, and strive with your wealth and your lives in the way of God.
look.prompt: What does 'strive' seem to mean in each verse? What clues, such as date or surrounding verses, point to one meaning over another?

check.q: What does the Arabic word jihad mean at its root?
choices: Holy war
Prayer
Striving or struggle
Pilgrimage
check.why: Jihad means striving; the Qur'an uses qital for fighting specifically, and 'holy war' has no exact Arabic original.

check.q: How do many hadith scholars rate the 'greater jihad' report?
choices: As the most reliable hadith of all
As a verse of the Qur'an
As a saying of Abu Bakr
As weak or unfounded, though Sufi and popular writers still cite it
check.why: Ibn Taymiyya and others judged the report weak; it remains popular for its spirit.

check.q: In classical Sunni law, who could declare armed jihad?
choices: A legitimate ruler, as a duty of the state
Any individual Muslim
Only a Sufi master
Only the Byzantine emperor
check.why: Law manuals placed jihad among the duties of the state; private individuals could not declare war.

lessons.title: Rulers, Consultation and Justice
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an gives no form of government but praises consultation, commands justice even against oneself, and ties authority to trust.
reading: The Qur'an names no constitution. It does not say 'caliph' in the political sense, does not describe an election, and does not lay out a state. What it does is set values. Verse 42:38, in a surah called Ash-Shura, 'Consultation,' praises those whose affairs are decided by *shura*, mutual consultation. Verse 3:159, Al Imran, tells the Prophet to consult his companions in matters and then, once resolved, to trust in God. Muslim tradition records him doing so before the battle of Uhud in 625, and losing the vote.

Justice is commanded repeatedly. Verse 4:58, An-Nisa, tells believers to restore trusts to their owners and to judge justly when they judge between people. Verse 4:135 tells them to stand firm for justice as witnesses for God even against themselves, their parents or their kin, whether the person is rich or poor. Verse 5:8 goes further: do not let hatred of a people move you away from justice; be just, for that is nearer to piety. Commentators from al-Tabari on have read that verse as binding toward enemies.

From these verses, and from the first four caliphs' examples as tradition tells them, Muslim political thinkers built very different theories. Medieval jurists such as al-Mawardi (d. 1058) described a caliph chosen by the community's leaders and bound by the law. Shia thinkers held that rightful leadership belonged to the Imams. Modern writers have argued that shura points to democracy, or to consultation within a monarchy, or to a council of scholars, each citing the same verses. Historians of political thought note that the text underdetermines all of these; the choice is made by the reader's other commitments.

What the verses do fix, most readers agree, is that authority is a trust, that rulers are under the law, and that justice is owed to everyone, including opponents. Muslim reformers in every century, from medieval jurists writing against tyranny to modern movements for accountable government, have cited 4:58 and 4:135 for this reason.

words.d: consultation; praised in 42:38 and commanded to the Prophet in 3:159
in 4:58, what must be restored to its owners; read by many as making authority itself a trust
a jurist (d. 1058) who wrote the classic Sunni description of the caliph's office

look.title: Even Against Yourselves
look.text: Verse 4:135 tells believers to stand firm for justice, as witnesses for God, even if it be against themselves, their parents or their kin, and whether the person concerned is rich or poor; it warns them not to follow desire so as to swerve, and says that if they distort or refuse, God is aware of what they do.
look.cite: Qur'an 4:135, An-Nisa, paraphrased from Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: What would it look like, in a court or a government, to follow this verse? Why might reformers in many centuries have found it useful?

check.q: What does the Qur'an say about the form of government?
choices: It commands a republic with elections
It names no form; it sets values such as consultation, justice and trust
It commands hereditary monarchy
It describes a parliament in Medina
check.why: The text underdetermines the form of state; readers have drawn democracy, monarchy and rule by scholars from the same verses.

check.q: What does 5:8 add to the command to be just?
choices: That justice applies only among Muslims
That judges must be from the Prophet's family
That hatred of a people must not move believers away from justice
That consultation replaces justice
check.why: 5:8 extends justice even to those one hates; commentators read it as binding toward enemies.

check.q: What does Muslim tradition report about the Prophet and consultation before Uhud in 625?
choices: He refused to consult anyone
He consulted the Byzantine emperor
He held the first election in Arabia
He consulted his companions and followed the majority view over his own
check.why: The sira reports that he preferred to defend from inside Medina but followed the majority who wanted to meet the enemy outside.

sections.title: The Earth, and the Answers to Extremism

lessons.title: Stewards of the Earth
lessons.mainIdea: The Qur'an calls humans God's khalifa, or steward, on earth, sets a balance in creation, and warns against waste, verses that Muslim environmental thinkers now cite.
reading: In 2:30, Al-Baqarah, God tells the angels that he is placing a *khalifa* on the earth. Pickthall's 1930 translation renders the word 'viceroy'; others say 'successor' or 'steward.' The angels ask whether God will place there one who will do harm and shed blood, and God answers that he knows what they do not. Classical commentators read the khalifa as Adam and his descendants, given charge of the earth on God's behalf. Modern Muslim environmental writers, from the 1960s on, have read the verse as a charge of stewardship: the earth is held in trust, not owned.

Surah 55, Ar-Rahman, 'The Merciful,' says in verses 7–9 that God raised the sky and set the *mizan*, the balance, and tells people not to transgress the balance but to keep it with justice. Surah 7:31, Al-A'raf, tells believers to eat and drink but not to be wasteful, adding that God does not love the wasteful. Surah 21:30, Al-Anbiya, says that God made every living thing from water. These verses, together with the Qur'an's repeated call to look at rain, seeds, bees and cattle as signs, are the core of a modern Muslim ecology.

In August 2015, Muslim scholars and leaders meeting in Istanbul issued the Islamic Declaration on Global Climate Change, which cited 2:30, 55:7–9 and 7:31 and called on Muslims and their governments to cut fossil fuel use. Islamic environmental groups in the United States, including in the Chicago area, run mosque recycling and energy programs and cite the same verses. The hadith literature adds reports of the Prophet forbidding the waste of water even at a flowing river and planting trees.

Historians of the tradition note that these readings are new emphases on old verses. Medieval jurists wrote about water rights, protected grazing zones called hima and cruelty to animals, but not about a planet in crisis. Whether the Qur'an 'teaches environmentalism' is therefore a question about how a living tradition reads its book for a new problem, which is exactly what this unit has been studying.

words.d: in 2:30, the one God places on the earth; rendered 'viceroy,' 'successor' or 'steward'
the balance that 55:7–9 says God set and people must not transgress
a protected zone, such as grazing land, in classical Islamic law

look.title: A Viceroy in the Earth
look.text: And when thy Lord said unto the angels: Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth, they said: Wilt thou place therein one who will do harm therein and will shed blood, while we, we hymn Thy praise and sanctify Thee? He said: Surely I know that which ye know not.
look.cite: Qur'an 2:30, Al-Baqarah, Marmaduke Pickthall, The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, 1930
look.prompt: Pickthall chose 'viceroy,' a ruler acting for a king. Others choose 'steward' or 'successor.' How does each English word change what the verse asks of humans?

check.q: How do modern Muslim environmental writers read 2:30?
choices: As making humans stewards who hold the earth in trust
As permission to use the earth however people wish
As a verse about the caliphs of Baghdad
As a verse about fasting
check.why: The khalifa is read as steward or trustee; classical commentators read it as Adam and his descendants.

check.q: What does 55:7–9 tell people to do?
choices: Build a mosque in every town
Keep the balance with justice and not transgress it
Eat only meat
Recite Surah 55 daily
check.why: The verses describe the mizan, the balance God set, and command that it be kept.

check.q: What did the 2015 Istanbul declaration do?
choices: Abolished the four schools of law
Declared a new caliphate
Cited Qur'anic verses to call for action on climate change
Banned all animal farming
check.why: The Islamic Declaration on Global Climate Change, issued in Istanbul in August 2015, quoted 2:30, 55:7–9 and 7:31.

lessons.title: How Extremists Read, and How Scholars Answer
lessons.mainIdea: Extremist groups quote verses out of context and bypass the tradition's rules; mainstream scholars answer by restoring the occasion, the surrounding verses and the law.
reading: Groups such as al-Qaeda and the self-declared Islamic State have quoted the Qur'an to justify attacks on civilians. Their method, as scholars who study their texts describe it, has a pattern. They quote 9:5 without verses 4, 6 and 13. They claim that the sword verse abrogated every verse of restraint. They declare that any Muslim who disagrees is not a Muslim, a practice called *takfir*, and that fighting can be declared by anyone, not only a legitimate authority. They treat the medieval dhimmi rules as binding today and the classical protections of noncombatants as void.

Mainstream scholars have answered in public, in detail and often. In September 2014, more than 120 Muslim scholars from many countries signed an open letter to the leader of the Islamic State. It went point by point: it is forbidden in Islam to issue rulings without full knowledge of the sources; to ignore the context of a verse; to kill the innocent, emissaries or journalists; to declare people non-Muslims unless they openly declare unbelief; to declare a caliphate without the consent of all Muslims; and to harm or mistreat Christians or any People of the Book. Each point cited verses and classical jurists.

The answer rests on the same tools this unit has studied. Occasion: 9:5 addresses treaty-breakers in 631. Context: verse 6 grants protection to anyone who asks. Abrogation: most scholars deny that 9:5 cancelled 2:190 or 8:61. Authority: no private person may declare war. Rules: noncombatants are protected, always. Takfir: a hadith reports the Prophet warning that whoever calls a Muslim an unbeliever brings the charge back on himself. Scholars from Al-Azhar, from Shia seminaries and from the Salafi movement itself have made versions of this argument.

None of this settles who is 'really' a Muslim, which is not a question a public school can answer. What it does show is that the tradition has an inside: a method, a body of rules and a community of readers, and that the argument against extremism is made, most of all, from within it. A student who has read this unit can now follow that argument and see what each side is doing with the text.

lessons.title: Amman and A Common Word
lessons.mainIdea: Two modern documents, the Amman Message of 2004 and A Common Word of 2007, show Muslim leaders publicly stating how they read the Qur'an on who is a Muslim and on love of God and neighbor.
reading: In November 2004, King Abdullah II of Jordan issued a statement written with senior scholars, known as the *Amman Message*. It described Islam as a religion of mercy and justice and rejected extremism. In July 2005, scholars from many countries met in Amman and agreed on three points: that followers of eight named schools of law, the four Sunni schools, the Ja'fari and Zaydi Shia schools, the Ibadi school and the Zahiri school, are all Muslims and may not be declared unbelievers; that takfir against them is forbidden; and that only qualified scholars, following a school's method, may issue fatwas. By later counts, more than five hundred scholars and leaders had endorsed the three points.

In October 2007, 138 Muslim scholars, leaders and thinkers sent an open letter to the Pope and the heads of the Christian churches. Its title, *A Common Word Between Us and You*, came from Qur'an 3:64, Al Imran, which calls the People of the Book to a common word: to worship none but God. The letter argued that love of God and love of neighbor are the shared foundation of both faiths, quoting the Qur'an on God's oneness and on justice to neighbors, and the Gospels' two great commandments. It asked for peace between the two largest religious communities on earth.

Christian leaders replied in large numbers; Yale, Cambridge and Georgetown hosted conferences on the letter, and church bodies issued formal responses. Scholars who study the document note that it uses the Qur'an's own method of addressing the People of the Book, quoting 3:64 exactly as the Qur'an frames an invitation, and that it was signed across Sunni and Shia lines. Critics inside and outside Islam have questioned how much it changed on the ground. Both the document and the criticism are part of the record.

Together the two documents make a fitting end to a unit on the Qur'an and law. They show a tradition using its own text and rules to say, in public, who belongs, who may speak for it, and how it wishes to stand toward other faiths. A student can read them as primary sources: what they cite, what they claim, whom they address, and what they leave open.
